human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper proposes SynTime, a syntactic-type-driven rule-based time-expression recognizer whose design is motivated by corpus observations (short expressions, small token set, consistent POS patterns). SynTime initializes a token/regex lexicon (reportedly from SUTime), groups tokens into syntactic types, identifies time tokens with regex+POS filtering, expands boundaries with left/right heuristics to include modifiers/numerals, and applies merge rules. Experiments on TimeBank, WikiWars, and a manually annotated Tweets set report high recall and competitive F1; manual expansion required few added tokens in these experiments.

Strengths:
- Empirical observations are clearly linked to design choices (Sections 3.2 and 4.1).
- The method is simple, interpretable, and easy to inspect/debug (Section 4.2; Figures 2–3).
- Reported recall performance is strong across datasets and aligns with the coverage-focused design (Table 4).
- The expansion workflow is practical and empirically required few added tokens per reported dataset (Table 5).

Limitations:
- Reproducibility gap: full token/regex lexica and implementation details (rule order/tie-breaking) are not provided; reproducing SynTime-I/E exactly is therefore infeasible from the manuscript alone.
- Comparative-evaluation uncertainty: some baseline numbers appear to be quoted from prior papers rather than re-run under the same preprocessing; without identical preprocessing, observed differences may not be attributable to algorithmic superiority.
- Tweets dataset selection bias: tweets were prefiltered using SUTime before annotation, risking biased test composition that could advantage SUTime-like lexical coverage and confound claims about tweet performance.
- Robustness and operational claims are unsupported quantitatively: no controlled experiments on POS/tagger sensitivity, no runtime/throughput/memory figures, and no annotation-effort/inter-annotator measures for expansion.

Open Questions:
- Please release the complete lexicon (token/regex lists per syntactic type) for SynTime-I and the additions used for SynTime-E; if privacy/proprietary restrictions apply, provide exhaustive appendices or a reconstruction script.
- Were baselines re-run locally under identical preprocessing? If not, rerun HeidelTime, SUTime, and UWTime under your pipeline and report results with bootstrap confidence intervals and statistical tests.
- How does performance change with different POS taggers (including a Twitter-specific tagger) and under controlled POS-tag noise? Please provide degradation curves or sensitivity analyses.
- Provide runtime benchmarks (ms per sentence or tweets/sec) and memory usage measured on a specified machine; clarify whether POS tagging time is included.
- For the Tweets dataset, can you provide an unbiased random-sample evaluation (no SUTime prefilter) or quantify SUTime false-negatives on a larger random sample to show selection-bias effects? 
- Provide expansion logs: the uncovered-word lists, add/reject decisions and rationales, annotator counts, inter-annotator agreement, and annotation time.

Transparency:
The manuscript currently lacks several artifacts that the community needs for reproducible verification: full lexica and regex inventories, preprocessing/evaluation scripts, local re-run logs for baselines, tweets sampling and annotation scripts, and expansion decision logs. Publishing these items will materially reduce uncertainty.

confidence_interval.rationale: Moderate confidence: reviewers consistently corroborate the descriptive corpus observations and the conceptual validity of a compact syntactic-type, boundary-expansion approach; reported in-pipeline empirical gains (high recall) are plausible. However, missing reproducibility artifacts (lexica, code), potential evaluation confounds (borrowed baseline numbers, SUTime-based tweet sampling), and absence of robustness/runtime analyses reduce confidence about the generality and operational claims. If authors supply the requested artifacts and reruns, confidence would rise toward the upper bound.

The underlying strategy in all the components is to find a pattern (from either a list or a previous process) which matches a rule, and then to apply the rule which annotates the text. Each component performs a particular process on the text, such as: sentence segmentation (dividing text into sentences); tokenization (words identified by spaces between them); part-of-speech tagging (noun, verb, adjective, etc., determined by look-up and relationships among words); shallow syntactic parsing/ chunking (dividing the text by noun phrase, verb phrase, subordinate clause, etc.); named entity recognition (NER) (the entities in the text such as organizations, people, and places); dependency analysis (subordinate clauses, pronominal anaphora [i.e., identifying what a pronoun refers to], etc.). The resulting process provides “structured” or semi-structured information to be further used (e.g. Knowledge Base building, Ontology enrichment, Machine Learning algorithm validation, Query Indexes for Question & Answer systems). Each component performs a particular process on the text, such as: sentence segmentation (dividing text into sentences); tokenization (words identified by spaces between them); part-of-speech tagging (noun, verb, adjective, etc., determined by look-up and relationships among words); shallow syntactic parsing/ chunking (dividing the text by noun phrase, verb phrase, subordinate clause, etc.); named entity recognition (NER) (the entities in the text such as organizations, people, and places); dependency analysis (subordinate clauses, pronominal anaphora [i.e., identifying what a pronoun refers to], etc.). Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The underlying strategy in all the components is to find a pattern (from either a list or a previous process) which matches a rule, and then to apply the rule which annotates the text. Each component performs a particular process on the text, such as: sentence segmentation (dividing text into sentences); tokenization (words identified by spaces between them); part-of-speech tagging (noun, verb, adjective, etc., determined by look-up and relationships among words); shallow syntactic parsing/ chunking (dividing the text by noun phrase, verb phrase, subordinate clause, etc.); named entity recognition (NER) (the entities in the text such as organizations, people, and places); dependency analysis (subordinate clauses, pronominal anaphora [i.e., identifying what a pronoun refers to], etc.). Some of the techniques that have been developed and can be used in the text mining process are information extraction, topic tracking, summarization, categorization, clustering, concept linkage, information visualization, question answering, and deep learning. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Then it would go through a text analysis phase, sometimes repeating techniques until information is extracted. The underlying strategy in all the components is to find a pattern (from either a list or a previous process) which matches a rule, and then to apply the rule which annotates the text. Each component performs a particular process on the text, such as: sentence segmentation (dividing text into sentences); tokenization (words identified by spaces between them); part-of-speech tagging (noun, verb, adjective, etc., determined by look-up and relationships among words); shallow syntactic parsing/ chunking (dividing the text by noun phrase, verb phrase, subordinate clause, etc.); named entity recognition (NER) (the entities in the text such as organizations, people, and places); dependency analysis (subordinate clauses, pronominal anaphora [i.e., identifying what a pronoun refers to], etc.). The resulting process provides “structured” or semi-structured information to be further used (e.g. Knowledge Base building, Ontology enrichment, Machine Learning algorithm validation, Query Indexes for Question & Answer systems). Some of the techniques that have been developed and can be used in the text mining process are information extraction, topic tracking, summarization, categorization, clustering, concept linkage, information visualization, question answering, and deep learning. Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
